sections.overview: The whooper swan is a large migratory waterbird of northern Eurasia, with white plumage, a long upright neck and ringing calls; it breeds from Iceland to Siberia and winters farther south.
sections.identification: Adults are 1.4–1.65 m long with a 2.05–2.75 m wingspan. Males weigh 7.4–14 kg (mean 9.8 kg), while females weigh 8.2–9.2 kg; a male’s neck is usually longer and thinner. Adults measure about 140–165 cm long and span 205–275 cm; males are heavier, and their black bill bears more yellow than the smaller, mostly black-billed Bewick’s swan.
sections.habitat: It nests beside shallow lakes and marshes in Eurasian taiga and subarctic tundra, where waterside vegetation offers cover; wintering birds also use estuaries, sheltered coasts and farmland.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on aquatic leaves, shoots, stems and roots, reaching plants with its long neck or by tipping forward; in winter it also grazes grass and crops, while small invertebrates are a minor food.
sections.behavior: Pairs defend territories while breeding, then gather in flocks; deep trumpet-like calls keep family members in contact, and head-bobbing can signal that birds are ready to take flight. Pairs usually remain together for life, and winter flocks contain families whose young migrate with their parents until the following breeding season.
sections.reproduction: Females lay four to seven eggs and incubate them about 35 days while males guard; downy cygnets leave the nest and fledge at roughly 78–105 days, depending on region. The nest is a mound of vegetation beside freshwater; the mobile young are nevertheless dependent on parental protection and help with feeding during their early development.
sections.ecology: Natural predators in northern Russia include red foxes, white-tailed eagles and golden eagles. Open water also supplies communal roosts for winter flocks. Predation affects eggs and small young most strongly; adults can retreat into water to escape terrestrial predators, while the parents’ vigilance protects the brood.
sections.conservation: The global IUCN assessment of 5 June 2025 lists the species as Least Concern, estimates 176,000 mature individuals and an increasing trend, while identifying wetland loss, disturbance, hunting, lead poisoning and power-line collisions as threats. Persecution reduced numbers and range in the 19th and early 20th centuries; bans on hunting later brought recovery.
